I'm Harish, and I sat behind Samir in class during the scholarship weeks. Samir wrote every step on the back of a notebook: certificates, the income form, the essay, the last date.
On Tuesday I saw Samir laying out the papers and going through them a second time, line by line. Then Samir took the essay to Mrs Deshmukh, the maths teacher, who read it and circled two spelling errors and a wrong date.
"It's a big form," Samir told me. "If I make a mistake, I can't change it after." I asked why not just send it. Samir said, "It isn't like a class test." The form went in two days before the deadline.

qa.q: Why did Samir check the papers twice, in Samir's own words?

qa.q: What could Samir add to the plan if there were even more time?
qa.a: Samir could ask a second person to read the form fresh, since a new reader may catch errors that Samir and the teacher missed.

qa.q: How might Mrs Deshmukh see the request to review the essay?
qa.a: Mrs Deshmukh was asked to read something important, and by finding a wrong date and two errors was clearly useful, so may feel glad to have helped.

Monday: Vasudha opened the scholarship form for a state science programme. The deadline was in three weeks. She thought, "If I miss one document, there's no second chance this year. So no rushing." She made a list: forms, marksheets, income certificate, two photos, school letter, essay. She gave each a date.

Tuesday of the second week: She checked every document twice against the instructions. The income certificate had her father's name misspelt. She got it corrected at the office. Her friend Nikita laughed. "You're so careful!" "This one can't go wrong," Vasudha said.

The following Monday: She asked her science teacher to read her essay. The teacher found two errors. Vasudha fixed them and submitted four days early.

qa.q: What was misspelt on the income certificate?
Why was Vasudha so careful with this application?
qa.a: She felt it was high-stakes and was anxious not to lose her one chance this year, so she didn't rush.

qa.q: Why did careful planning suit this task?
qa.a: Errors here were costly and hard to undo, so listing steps, checking twice and getting a review was worth the time.

qa.q: How does Nikita see Vasudha's care?
qa.a: Nikita finds it amusing at first, perhaps thinking it's too much, but it caught a real error.

passage: Vandana, when you apply for that scholarship, remember what your Kavitha Aunty did at your age. I was sixteen, and it was a scholarship for a residential school in the city. For most things, I was careless. But I thought, "If I make one mistake here, they won't call. No second chance." So I did it differently. I wrote every step in a notebook with dates. I checked each certificate against the list twice, and found my birth certificate had the wrong year. I went to the municipal office three times to get it right. Then I asked my headmaster to read my form. He found one blank I had missed. I got the scholarship. Careless is fine for small things, beta. Not this.

qa.q: What was wrong with young Kavitha's birth certificate?
What did young Kavitha feel about this application compared with other things?
qa.a: She felt the stakes were high and was anxious not to lose her one chance, so she was careful here though careless elsewhere.

qa.q: At what point in the story did Kavitha's care pay off most?
qa.a: When checking the certificates twice and asking the headmaster; both caught errors that could have cost her the scholarship.

qa.q: How might the headmaster have seen Kavitha asking him to check?
qa.a: He probably respected her seriousness and was glad to help catch the blank she missed.
